speaker.intro: Two members of “Jeonseol Iljido”, the team that won the Grand Prize at last year’s CUIF+, share how they prepared in an interview. We split one 12-minute video by topic, and the video attached to each section starts playing right where that story begins. The summary below gives the main points of the video, so please watch the video for their exact words and mood.

guideQuote.title: The one sentence running through this video
guideQuote.body: Don’t get trapped inside the given topics — plan something sharp and concise enough that a local public official says “We’d use this.”

chapters.title: Team introduction — plan together, split making and presenting
chapters.lead: How the 2025 CUIF+ Grand Prize team “Jeonseol Iljido” divided its roles

c: 2025 CUIF+ **Grand Prize** team “Jeonseol Iljido” — a five-person team including Choi Junhyeok
**Planning and flow, all together** — they traded ideas and set the overall flow as a team
**Making centred on one person** — one design member did most of the production
**Presenting by Choi Junhyeok** — the very alumnus who wrote “TIPS for winning (grand) prizes in competitions” on this site

blocks.c: **Planning is everyone’s job, but split the hands** — think together, but decide in advance who makes and who speaks.

chapters.title: Choosing a topic — look “outside” the 9 topics
chapters.lead: Pick the city, but dig up the problem yourselves

c: Since it’s a competition, they started from **topics other teams wouldn’t touch**
If you only choose within the 9 topics, your thinking gets limited → they **researched deeply** to find ideas others wouldn’t come up with
They picked just one city, **Yeoncheon**, and **found the detailed topic themselves**
They **visited Yeoncheon in person** and went around many places, then decided “none of the given topics can be solved with a student idea” and set a new topic

blocks.c: **Can a student’s idea actually solve this?** — if there’s no answer when you ask that, find a new topic.
Choosing the topic took a long time, but they say **once they locked in one idea and concept**, the rest wasn’t hard.

chapters.title: Planning — sharp and concise
chapters.lead: Time allocation · Check questions · Where to find references

c: CUIF needs feasibility too, but **persuasiveness** is the key → centred on “who can we show our story to most persuasively,” they spent **a long time on setting the target** and scrapped a lot
Even around the mid-point hackathon, **nothing was decided** — they kept scrapping topics
They spent **more than half of all their time on choosing the topic**
Design also takes long when one person makes many pages → they **allocated production time in advance**

blocks.c: What they cared about in planning

c: They kept asking “Isn’t this **an obvious idea other teams could also think of?**” and made it as sharp as possible
Because it wasn’t a given topic, they had to persuade with logic **why this topic is needed and what makes it different** → they put effort into the flow of the plan
But if the plan **gets long** while trying to show logic, **it’s not a good plan** → cut unnecessary words and use **concise wording**
The design member thought most about “how can we show our idea **in the coolest way**”
In the planning stage, **research was the most important**
Look at lots of **winning entries** from big competitions run by major ad agencies and **related news articles** → ideas like “what if we use this and change it like this?” come out
For design, they referred to winners of big competitions and portfolio sites like **Pinterest·Behance**
✅ Planning check questions
Could other teams also come up with this idea?
Can you explain in one flow why this topic is needed “in this region, now”?
Are there any sentences left that still make sense if you remove them?

chapters.title: Team meetings — how to clash the right way
chapters.lead: Clash, but bring an alternative with criticism · Meet face to face

c: **Don’t hesitate to disagree** — “I think this is better,” “the earlier one seemed better,” “what if we change it like this?” You have to cut and cut and cut to get a better idea
If there are one or two people with strong opinions, clashes are bound to happen → you need **someone to mediate in the middle**
If an option you don’t like comes up, don’t end with “not great” — bring **why it’s not great together with another option** — criticism without reasons is not okay
Instead of worrying “Am I helping the team?”, **do your best so you won’t regret it later** — CUIF is a competition where every single team member matters

blocks.c: Please, meet in person, not online

They say when you meet face to face, personal chat mixes in, **your focus goes up**, and you can **speak freely** without feeling small. This is the part both alumni stressed as “really, really important.”
**When you criticise, bring an alternative.** Disagreement is a tool for sharpening ideas, not for cutting down people.

chapters.title: Through the judges’ eyes — think like a public official
chapters.lead: A “plus alpha” on current policy · Keep the concept to one line to the end

c: Build your idea **from the local public official’s point of view, not the student’s** — some of the judges are public officials too
“If I were a public official, **would I really use** this idea?”
Think one step further, as a **plus alpha on a policy already in place**
The target is **a region**, not an ad, so the concept must carry through to the end — if it doesn’t, the idea looks **scattered**

blocks.c: Don’t treat it like a light on-campus contest
Many **outside judges** come to CUIF, and they evaluate **precisely with score sheets**. So they say you need to prepare more seriously, gathering together as a team, to get good results.
**“Could our city use this idea starting tomorrow?”** — if you can answer “yes” to this, you’re halfway there.

chapters.title: For first-timers
chapters.lead: Learning over prizes · When a plan falls apart · CUIF in one word

blocks.c: Don’t enter just to win a prize

c: The first time, they thought “maybe at least an Encouragement Award…”, but on the day they saw their plan was really not good — a plan they never open again now
If it’s your first time, think of it as time to learn **how to write a plan, how the PT (presentation) goes, and where your plan went wrong**
After that failure, they prepared **with gritted teeth** the next year and won the **Grand Prize** — “we won’t repeat what we did last year”

blocks.c: When you’re deep into your plan, there comes a time when everything you say **seems right and perfectly logical**. That is exactly when it falls apart. Check in with your **professor**, or with **seniors** if that feels like too much, from time to time: “Is this okay?”

c: “The foundation where I could grow the most” — at CUIF they learned how to plan, how to make, and how to **connect IMC to the concept**
Even with many hard and discouraging moments, don’t give up until the end
When you’re too tired, **refresh** with your teammates now and then — that’s how better ideas come

closing.quote: Looking back later, you’ll say “I got this far thanks to CUIF.”
paras: At first you may think “What do I do? I have no idea where to start.” But once you get in and actually try, how to plan, how to make, and how to tie an idea into a concept stay with you, one by one.

Just as the alumni who tasted a bitter first try won the Grand Prize the next year, **this preparation becomes the stepping stone for your next challenge**. Don’t worry too much, and go all the way with your team.
closing.sign: We wish you good results. Fighting! 🏆
